T1001.name: Data Obfuscation
T1001.desc: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.

T1001.001.name: Data Obfuscation: Junk Data
T1001.001.desc: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.

T1001.002.name: Data Obfuscation: Steganography
T1001.002.desc: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult.

T1001.003.name: Data Obfuscation: Protocol or Service Impersonation
T1001.003.desc: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts.

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.desc: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password.

T1003.001.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.desc: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).

T1003.002.name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.desc: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored.

T1003.003.name: OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
T1003.003.desc: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and a…

T1003.004.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.desc: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts.

T1003.005.name: OS Credential Dumping: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.desc: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.

T1003.006.name: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
T1003.006.desc: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain con…

T1005.name: Data from Local System
T1005.desc: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

T1006.name: Direct Volume Access
T1006.desc: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring.

T1007.name: System Service Discovery
T1007.desc: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services.

T1008.name: Fallback Channels
T1008.desc: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

T1010.name: Application Window Discovery
T1010.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows.

T1011.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
T1011.desc: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel.

T1011.001.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
T1011.001.desc: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel.

T1012.name: Query Registry
T1012.desc: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

T1014.name: Rootkit
T1014.desc: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components.

T1016.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
T1016.desc: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems.

T1016.001.name: System Network Configuration Discovery: Internet Connection Discovery
T1016.001.desc: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems.

T1016.002.name: System Network Configuration Discovery: Wi-Fi Discovery
T1016.002.desc: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems.

T1018.name: Remote System Discovery
T1018.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system.

T1020.name: Automated Exfiltration
T1020.desc: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.

T1021.name: Remote Services
T1021.desc: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC.

T1021.001.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
T1021.001.desc: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).

T1021.002.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
T1021.002.desc: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB).

T1021.003.name: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
T1021.003.desc: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM).

T1021.005.name: Remote Services: VNC
T1021.005.desc: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).

T1021.006.name: Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
T1021.006.desc: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM).

T1025.name: Data from Removable Media
T1025.desc: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

T1027.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
T1027.desc: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit.

T1027.001.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding
T1027.001.desc: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware.

T1027.002.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
T1027.002.desc: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code.

T1027.003.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Steganography
T1027.003.desc: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information.

T1027.004.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
T1027.004.desc: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code.

T1027.005.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from Tools
T1027.005.desc: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed.

T1027.006.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: HTML Smuggling
T1027.006.desc: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files.

T1027.007.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Dynamic API Resolution
T1027.007.desc: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis.

T1027.008.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Stripped Payloads
T1027.008.desc: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information.

T1027.009.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
T1027.009.desc: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses.

T1027.010.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
T1027.010.desc: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection.

T1027.011.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Fileless Storage
T1027.011.desc: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses.

T1027.012.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: LNK Icon Smuggling
T1027.012.desc: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files.

T1027.013.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
T1027.013.desc: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection.

T1027.014.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Polymorphic Code
T1027.014.desc: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection.

T1027.015.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compression
T1027.015.desc: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files.

T1027.016.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Junk Code Insertion
T1027.016.desc: Adversaries may use junk code / dead code to obfuscate a malware’s functionality.

T1027.017.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: SVG Smuggling
T1027.017.desc: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign SVG files.

T1027.018.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Invisible Unicode
T1027.018.desc: Adversaries may abuse invisible or non-printing Unicode characters to conceal malicious content within files, scripts, or text.

T1029.name: Scheduled Transfer
T1029.desc: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals.

T1030.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
T1030.desc: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds.

T1033.name: System Owner/User Discovery
T1033.desc: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system.

T1036.name: Masquerading
T1036.desc: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

T1036.001.name: Masquerading: Invalid Code Signature
T1036.001.desc: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool.

T1036.002.name: Masquerading: Right-to-Left Override
T1036.002.desc: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign.

T1036.003.name: Masquerading: Rename Legitimate Utilities
T1036.003.desc: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities.

T1036.004.name: Masquerading: Masquerade Task or Service
T1036.004.desc: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign.

T1036.005.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
T1036.005.desc: Adversaries may match or approximate the name or location of legitimate files, Registry keys, or other resources when naming/placing them.

T1036.007.name: Masquerading: Double File Extension
T1036.007.desc: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type.

T1036.008.name: Masquerading: Masquerade File Type
T1036.008.desc: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents.

T1036.010.name: Masquerading: Masquerade Account Name
T1036.010.desc: Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign.

T1036.012.name: Masquerading: Browser Fingerprint
T1036.012.desc: Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.

T1037.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
T1037.desc: Adversaries may use scripts automatically executed at boot or logon initialization to establish persistence.

T1037.001.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
T1037.001.desc: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

T1037.003.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Network Logon Script
T1037.003.desc: Adversaries may use network logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

T1039.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
T1039.desc: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.desc: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network.

T1041.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
T1041.desc: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel.

T1046.name: Network Service Discovery
T1046.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation.

T1047.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
T1047.desc: Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads.

T1048.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
T1048.desc: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

T1048.001.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
T1048.001.desc: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

T1048.002.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
T1048.002.desc: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

T1048.003.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
T1048.003.desc: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

T1049.name: System Network Connections Discovery
T1049.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems by querying for information over the network.

T1052.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
T1052.desc: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive.

T1052.001.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over USB
T1052.001.desc: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device.

T1053.name: Scheduled Task/Job
T1053.desc: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

T1053.002.name: Scheduled Task/Job: At
T1053.002.desc: Adversaries may abuse the at utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

T1053.005.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
T1053.005.desc: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

T1055.name: Process Injection
T1055.desc: Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.001.name: Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection
T1055.001.desc: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.002.name: Process Injection: Portable Executable Injection
T1055.002.desc: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PE) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.003.name: Process Injection: Thread Execution Hijacking
T1055.003.desc: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.004.name: Process Injection: Asynchronous Procedure Call
T1055.004.desc: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.005.name: Process Injection: Thread Local Storage
T1055.005.desc: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via thread local storage (TLS) callbacks in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.011.name: Process Injection: Extra Window Memory Injection
T1055.011.desc: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.012.name: Process Injection: Process Hollowing
T1055.012.desc: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses.

T1055.013.name: Process Injection: Process Doppelgänging
T1055.013.desc: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via process doppelgänging in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1055.015.name: Process Injection: ListPlanting
T1055.015.desc: Adversaries may abuse list-view controls to inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.desc: Adversaries may use methods of capturing user input to obtain credentials or collect information.

T1056.001.name: Input Capture: Keylogging
T1056.001.desc: Adversaries may log user keystrokes to intercept credentials as the user types them.

T1056.002.name: Input Capture: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.desc: Adversaries may mimic common operating system GUI components to prompt users for credentials with a seemingly legitimate prompt.

T1056.003.name: Input Capture: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.desc: Adversaries may install code on externally facing portals, such as a VPN login page, to capture and transmit credentials of users who attempt to log into the service.

T1056.004.name: Input Capture: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.desc: Adversaries may hook into Windows application programming interface (API) functions and Linux system functions to collect user credentials.

T1057.name: Process Discovery
T1057.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system.

T1059.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
T1059.desc: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries.

T1059.001.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1059.001.desc: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution.

T1059.003.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
T1059.003.desc: Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution.

T1059.005.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
T1059.005.desc: Adversaries may abuse Visual Basic (VB) for execution.

T1059.006.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
T1059.006.desc: Adversaries may abuse Python commands and scripts for execution.

T1059.007.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
T1059.007.desc: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution.

T1059.010.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: AutoHotKey & AutoIT
T1059.010.desc: Adversaries may execute commands and perform malicious tasks using AutoIT and AutoHotKey automation scripts.

T1059.011.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Lua
T1059.011.desc: Adversaries may abuse Lua commands and scripts for execution.

T1068.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
T1068.desc: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges.

T1069.name: Permission Groups Discovery
T1069.desc: Adversaries may attempt to discover group and permission settings.

T1069.001.name: Permission Groups Discovery: Local Groups
T1069.001.desc: Adversaries may attempt to find local system groups and permission settings.

T1069.002.name: Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups
T1069.002.desc: Adversaries may attempt to find domain-level groups and permission settings.

T1070.name: Indicator Removal
T1070.desc: Adversaries may selectively delete or modify artifacts generated to reduce indications of their presence and blend in with legitimate activity.

T1070.003.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Command History
T1070.003.desc: In addition to clearing system logs, an adversary may clear the command history of a compromised account to conceal the actions undertaken during an intrusion.

T1070.004.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
T1070.004.desc: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity.

T1070.005.name: Indicator Removal: Network Share Connection Removal
T1070.005.desc: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation.

T1070.006.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
T1070.006.desc: Adversaries may modify file time attributes to hide new files or changes to existing files.

T1070.007.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
T1070.007.desc: Adversaries may clear or remove evidence of malicious network connections in order to clean up traces of their operations.

T1070.008.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Mailbox Data
T1070.008.desc: Adversaries may modify mail and mail application data to remove evidence of their activity.

T1070.009.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Persistence
T1070.009.desc: Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity.

T1070.010.name: Indicator Removal: Relocate Malware
T1070.010.desc: Once a payload is delivered, adversaries may reproduce copies of the same malware on the victim system to remove evidence of their presence and/or avoid defenses.

T1071.name: Application Layer Protocol
T1071.desc: Adversaries may communicate using OSI application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

T1071.001.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1071.001.desc: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with web traffic to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

T1071.002.name: Application Layer Protocol: File Transfer Protocols
T1071.002.desc: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with transferring files to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

T1071.003.name: Application Layer Protocol: Mail Protocols
T1071.003.desc: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with electronic mail delivery to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

T1071.004.name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
T1071.004.desc: Adversaries may communicate using the Domain Name System (DNS) application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

T1071.005.name: Application Layer Protocol: Publish/Subscribe Protocols
T1071.005.desc: Adversaries may communicate using publish/subscribe (pub/sub) application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

T1072.name: Software Deployment Tools
T1072.desc: Adversaries may gain access to and use centralized software suites installed within an enterprise to execute commands and move laterally through the network.

T1074.name: Data Staged
T1074.desc: Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location or directory prior to Exfiltration.

T1074.001.name: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
T1074.001.desc: Adversaries may stage collected data in a central location or directory on the local system prior to Exfiltration.

T1074.002.name: Data Staged: Remote Data Staging
T1074.002.desc: Adversaries may stage data collected from multiple systems in a central location or directory on one system prior to Exfiltration.

T1078.name: Valid Accounts
T1078.desc: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

T1078.001.name: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts
T1078.001.desc: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a default account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

T1078.002.name: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
T1078.002.desc: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a domain account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

T1078.003.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
T1078.003.desc: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a local account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

T1080.name: Taint Shared Content
T1080.desc: Adversaries may deliver payloads to remote systems by adding content to shared storage locations, such as network drives or internal code repositories.

T1082.name: System Information Discovery
T1082.desc: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture.

T1083.name: File and Directory Discovery
T1083.desc: Adversaries may enumerate files and directories or may search in specific locations of a host or network share for certain information within a file system.

T1087.name: Account Discovery
T1087.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of valid accounts, usernames, or email addresses on a system or within a compromised environment.

T1087.001.name: Account Discovery: Local Account
T1087.001.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of local system accounts.

T1087.002.name: Account Discovery: Domain Account
T1087.002.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of domain accounts.

T1087.003.name: Account Discovery: Email Account
T1087.003.desc: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of email addresses and accounts.

T1090.name: Proxy
T1090.desc: Adversaries may use a connection proxy to direct network traffic between systems or act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure.

T1090.001.name: Proxy: Internal Proxy
T1090.001.desc: Adversaries may use an internal proxy to direct command and control traffic between two or more systems in a compromised environment.

T1090.002.name: Proxy: External Proxy
T1090.002.desc: Adversaries may use an external proxy to act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure.

T1090.003.name: Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy
T1090.003.desc: Adversaries may chain together multiple proxies to disguise the source of malicious traffic.

T1090.004.name: Proxy: Domain Fronting
T1090.004.desc: Adversaries may take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and other services which host multiple domains to obfuscate the intended destination of HTTPS traffic or traffic tunneled through HTT…

T1091.name: Replication Through Removable Media
T1091.desc: Adversaries may move onto systems, possibly those on disconnected or air-gapped networks, by copying malware to removable media and taking advantage of Autorun features when the media is inserted into a system and execu…

T1092.name: Communication Through Removable Media
T1092.desc: Adversaries can perform command and control between compromised hosts on potentially disconnected networks using removable media to transfer commands from system to system.

T1095.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
T1095.desc: Adversaries may use an OSI non-application layer protocol for communication between host and C2 server or among infected hosts within a network.

T1098.name: Account Manipulation
T1098.desc: Adversaries may manipulate accounts to maintain and/or elevate access to victim systems.

T1098.002.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
T1098.002.desc: Adversaries may grant additional permission levels to maintain persistent access to an adversary-controlled email account.

T1098.005.name: Account Manipulation: Device Registration
T1098.005.desc: Adversaries may register a device to an adversary-controlled account.

T1098.007.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups
T1098.007.desc: An adversary may add additional local or domain groups to an adversary-controlled account to maintain persistent access to a system or domain.

T1102.name: Web Service
T1102.desc: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for relaying data to/from a compromised system.

T1102.001.name: Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
T1102.001.desc: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to host information that points to additional command and control (C2) infrastructure.

T1102.002.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
T1102.002.desc: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel.

T1102.003.name: Web Service: One-Way Communication
T1102.003.desc: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to a compromised system without receiving return output over the Web service channel.

T1104.name: Multi-Stage Channels
T1104.desc: Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions.

T1105.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
T1105.desc: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment.

T1106.name: Native API
T1106.desc: Adversaries may interact with the native OS application programming interface (API) to execute behaviors.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.desc: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.

T1110.001.name: Brute Force: Password Guessing
T1110.001.desc: Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials within the system or environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts.

T1110.002.name: Brute Force: Password Cracking

T1552.002.name: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Registry

T1553.002.desc: Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools.

T1553.006.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
